articles.text: At its September 5 meeting, the City Council will discuss two proposals to make new housing easier to build in Piedmont with pre-approved design plans for affordable Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), and objective design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings. Accessory dwellings (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs, which are Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont, can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (Construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). The proposal would allow Piedmont property owners who submit these preapproved designs as-is to receive a planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the development process. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. However, the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing homeowners to submit ADUs larger than a standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Information on the permit-ready ADU styles, and larger ADUs is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Multifamily objective design standards (MODS) Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The MODS don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. generally urban infill areas, which comprise less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking – they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Community members may submit comments on the proposals ahead of the meeting by email to PiedmontIsHome@piedmont. ca.gov; by mail to the Piedmont Planning Commission, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or speak on the topic at the 5:30 p.m. August 14 meeting in-person or via Zoom. The agenda report for both items is available for download on PiedmontIsHome.org. articles.text: Staff photo The bollards at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue are expected to be replaced by a permanent traffic island. A new traffic and safety design plan will lead to the removal of bollards currently at the intersection of Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue. The project will go out to bid in late September, with construction expected to start in January 2024 and finish that summer. The current painted-stripe “bollard island” at the intersection was approved by the City Council in April 2019, but has come under fire from neighbors. It will be replaced by a permanent, curb-defined traffic island with a pedestrian crosswalk through it. The island will provide direction to westbound drivers on Magnolia. The plan also includes an eastbound left turn pocket to allow sight distance for vehicles turning left from Magnolia onto Nova. The traffic island will be treated with mulch to allow for landscaping upgrades, and will be shaped to allow driveway access for all neighboring residents. A bulb-out will also be added to the 101 corner of Magnolia for traffic making the turn downhill and right onto Nova. The plan will not restrict or eliminate any currently available street parking. The Council approved the new traffic and safety design plan at its April 3, 2023, meeting. The total estimated construction cost is $100,000. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the project “goes back at least 10 years.” The current cluster of bollards met with protests from local residents who contended it was unsightly, confused drivers, and did little to protect pedestrians. In May 2022, one year ago, 120 residents signed a petition asking the city to make permanent improvements to the intersection. Gonzales said that, since then, Public Works held “many public meetings … and a number of follow up meetings with individuals who are impacted by the project, both one on one and then in small neighborhood working groups,” particularly in summer 2022. The meetings focused on traffic impact, pedestrian counts, maintaining access to driveways, and maintaining adequate sight distance for drivers turning left onto Nova from Magnolia. He said that this new plan for a permanent traffic island was made after the meetings and “generally … was very well received.” Questions and comments about the plan may be directed to Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov or phone at 420-3061. Multifamily objective design standards (MODS) Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The MODS don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. generally urban infill areas, which comprise less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking – they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is thrilled to announce that contributions to its fund to provide sustainable landscaping and to support the city’s effort to use green infrastructure for the community swimming pool have passed the $100,000 mark, thereby fully utilizing PBF’s $100,000 matching grant announced this spring. The funds will go toward completion of the new pool’s landscaping with elements and plantings that are both aesthetically appealing and ecologically sensitive. As of August 16, PBF has received contributions totaling $111,611. It is not too late for citizens to add to that total. PBF plans to publish the names of donors as of September 30; thus, there is plenty of time for everyone to become supporters of this landmark project. When informed of the success of the campaign to date, Eric Havian, a leader of the PRFO campaign to fill the original funding gap for the pool, had the following to say: “PBF’s extraordinary contributions have been most valuable because they send a message to the entire City that the value of the Community Pool is not limited to sports groups. The unprecedented support of civic organizations like PBF demonstrates to our residents that everyone will benefit from this jewel in the center of Piedmont. PRFO is profoundly grateful to PBF for stepping up in such a major way.” PBF has been a supporter of the pool from the beginning. It endorsed Measure UU, the bond measure providing the major funding for the pool. When bids came in higher than anticipated, the PBF Trustees voted to contribute $25,000 to help kick off PRFO’s campaign to fill the gap. Now, with the success of the matching grant campaign, Bob McBain, a former mayor and PBF member was delighted, saying, “I’m very grateful that PBF was an early and enthusiastic supporter of the pool project, and has now encouraged others to make contributions to make the pool an amazing facility.” With over $236,000 having now been contributed or pledged toward the pool, PBF hopes its total support may reach a quarter of a million dollars. The sustainable landscaping that PBF will fund will bring native plants and green infrastructure to the pool facility that will conserve water and reduce runoff and pollution. The plants will build the soil and provide habitat for birds and pollinators. This is clearly in line with PBF’s motto: “PBF in partnership with the City for a Safe, Sustainable and Beautiful Community.” Contributions to the pool landscaping campaign can still be sent to PBF at City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611- 4301. Or via the PBF website at www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org.

articles.text: 6 student-teachers gaining credentials and Master’s degrees Some Piedmont students might find a second teacher in some of their classrooms this year, as the district now has six “Alder Resident” student-teachers. The Alder Graduate School of Education’s teacher residency program allows prospective individuals to earn their teaching credential and Master’s degree in one year while being mentored by a credentialed teacher. This year, four Alder Residents will be at Piedmont High and two are teaching at the elementary schools. The program is similar to Teach For America but at the state and local levels, not through a national program. Alder Residents are contracted through the Alameda County Office of Education (ACOE), which provides each with a $30,000 stipend. A wide range of grant, loan and scholarship options open up to student-teachers once they are accepted into the Alder Graduate School teacher resident program which costs $21,000 in tuition. Piedmont Alder Residents took one month of in-person classes at College of Alameda this summer. During their fall and spring semesters they concurrently take courses to earn a Master’s degree and teaching credential. By next year they will be certified. At PHS, Alder Resident Caleb Brown is paired with Dave Keller (Social Science), Norma Juarez (Spanish) teaches under Deysi Sahagon, Beth McNeill is in John Hayden’s math classroom and Lael Melchert is learning the ins and out of Biology lessons from Shelley Seto. Two more Alder residents are working with Piedmont elementary school special education teachers. Bunthoeun Hack works under Michelle Sage at Beach School, and Kwame Payne is learning on the job from Sally Samuth at Havens. Payne, Hack and McNeil worked in the district last year as classified staff or as substitute teachers. McNeil, also a mom of two Beach students, started to seriously explore a career in teaching at the start of 2023 by substitute teaching. She ended up finishing the school year as a long-term substitute for a Beach Kindergarten teacher on maternity leave for six weeks. McNeil told the Post there are plenty of options to get a credential but was drawn towards the Alder program because it gives her a Master’s degree and because it lets you work with a teacher in the classroom for a full year. She currently is the student-teacher in Hayden’s honors statistics and Math Analysis classes. “The program gives you a lot of freedom, and it can change every day. On Thursday I am doing a take-over of a couple classes,” she said. McNeil said other teachers in the math department have given her the green light to sit in on their lessons, too. PUSD’s Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich oversees the Alder Residents. He confirmed that the program gives the district a leg up on hiring new teachers, something critical during the current teacher shortage. “Superintendent Hawn and I both love the idea of the Alder Resident program; we need to grow that,” said Dolowich. A success story of the program is Piedmont native Russell Jeng (PHS 2014), who was mentored by 2nd grade teacher Nancy Roscelli last year, Roscelli’s final year of teaching before retirement. Jeng was hired as a certified 3rd grade teacher at Beach for the fall, where he teaches math, writing and science. “Teaching in Piedmont has been great, it’s wonderful to see how much these kids know and knowing that I was once in their footsteps a long time ago,” he said. “I would recommend this program. It’s intense and you’ll really need to be committed, but having a mentor and residency director will give you someone who you can always turn to for advice and help,” said Jeng. Current Alder Resident Beth McNeil is earning her teaching credential and Master’s degree while receiving in-class experience and mentorship at PHS. pages.text: Wednesday, August 30, 2023 7 Alder Resident program brings student teachers to Piedmont 6 student-teachers gaining credentials and Master’s degrees By Jay Russell Some Piedmont students might find a second teacher in some of their classrooms this year, as the district now has six “Alder Resident” student-teachers. The Alder Graduate School of Education’s teacher residency program allows prospective individuals to earn their teaching credential and Master’s degree in one year while being mentored by a credentialed teacher. This year, four Alder Residents will be at Piedmont High and two are teaching at the elementary schools. The program is similar to Teach For America but at the state and local levels, not through a national program. Alder Residents are contracted through the Alameda County Office of Education (ACOE), which provides each with a $30,000 stipend. A wide range of grant, loan and scholarship options open up to student-teachers once they are accepted into the Alder Graduate School teacher resident program which costs $21,000 in tuition. Piedmont Alder Residents took one month of in-person classes at College of Alameda this summer. During their fall and spring semesters they concurrently take courses to earn a Master’s degree and teaching credential. By next year they will be certified. At PHS, Alder Resident Caleb Brown is paired with Dave Keller (Social Science), Norma Juarez (Spanish) teaches under Deysi Sahagon, Beth McNeill is in John Hayden’s math classroom and Lael Melchert is learning the ins and out of Biology lessons from Shelley Seto. Two more Alder residents are working with Piedmont elementary school special education teachers. Bunthoeun Hack works under Michelle Sage at Beach School, and Kwame Payne is learning on the job from Sally Samuth at Havens. Payne, Hack and McNeil worked in the district last year as classified staff or as substitute teachers. McNeil, also a mom of two Beach students, started to seriously explore a career in teaching at the start of 2023 by substitute teaching. She ended up finishing the school year as a long-term substitute for a Beach Kindergarten teacher on maternity leave for six weeks. McNeil told the Post there are plenty of options to get a credential but was drawn towards the Alder program because it gives her a Master’s degree and because it lets you work with a teacher in the classroom for a full year. She currently is the student-teacher in Hayden’s honors statistics and Math Analysis classes. “The program gives you a lot of freedom, and it can change every day. On Thursday I am doing a take-over of a couple classes,” she said. McNeil said other teachers in the math department have given her the green light to sit in on their lessons, too. PUSD’s Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich oversees the Alder Residents. He confirmed that the program gives the district a leg up on hiring new teachers, something critical during the current teacher shortage. “Superintendent Hawn and I both love the idea of the Alder Resident program; we need to grow that,” said Dolowich. A success story of the program is Piedmont native Russell Jeng (PHS 2014), who was mentored by 2nd grade teacher Nancy Roscelli last year, Roscelli’s final year of teaching before retirement. Jeng was hired as a certified 3rd grade teacher at Beach for the fall, where he teaches math, writing and science. “Teaching in Piedmont has been great, it’s wonderful to see how much these kids know and knowing that I was once in their footsteps a long time ago,” he said. “I would recommend this program. It’s intense and you’ll really need to be committed, but having a mentor and residency director will give you someone who you can always turn to for advice and help,” said Jeng. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is ready to take on another great year of service. The Crew, a coed Venturing program through the Piedmont Scout Council, will host an Open House on September 10 to describe its many activities and projects taking place during the year. PCSC has been around for 19 years, providing a chance for generations of local youth (ages 10-20) to plan, participate in, and contribute to projects. It is a fun and easy way to get service hours while establishing bonds with fellow Crew members. While we do not impose any participation minimums, to keep it a low-stress organization, our members provide their own ideas on how to make community service beneficial to all. We confidently say that everything that we do as a crew is amazing. We plan and create our unique projects that interest us, often funding the costs as well. Many of our most popular events were originated and conceived by past members,” said Elena O’Connell, Vice President of Communications. A small sampling includes: sorting produce at the Alameda County Community Food Bank, cooking meals for the food insecure, painting murals, building Tiny Houses for homeless teens, improving and cleaning the local environment, and tutoring children, The Community Service Crew has roughly 150 members and organize multiple events each week. It provide leadership opportunities for its members, and a platform to share their own ideas, building self confidence in the process. Every spring the most involved members are encouraged to run for elected positions. The elected crew officers are mentored weekly by adult volunteers to take on responsibilities that are often associated only with adults. The VPs each lead their own team of assistants and are responsible for different aspects of running an organization. Cooking for the food insecure — Members enjoy the teamwork involved in cooking together, and one member takes on the planning of the menu and shopping for the food. We do this more than once per month. The crew’s fundraising team provides funding. Tutoring underserved elementary school kids — PCSC piloted a new weekly program with an East Oakland elementary school to help children from Spanish speaking families. Crew members sign up for each Wednesday that they are available; parents are needed to drive. Tiny House project — PCSC has funded and built several tiny houses for homeless teens over the past few years and is excited to start on a new project this September. We hope to raise $10,000 via donations in the next few weeks, then build the house on a trailer in Piedmont and deliver it to a new Tiny House village in Richmond. Crew members will be encouraged to work on weekends. Annual House Renovation project — Each spring, a select team of members form a project team working with Rebuilding Together Oakland to select a low income, elderly or disabled Oakland homeowner whose home will be renovated. The crew typically spends 3 months on the project and over a thousand hours. PCSC is one of very few volunteer groups that manages its project independently, and the only teen group doing that. Fundraising in the community — Our Fundraising VPs organize several fundraising events that give the crew visibility in our community. PCSC is a proud sponsor of the annual Piedmont July 4th pancake breakfast, a major fundraiser for future projects.

articles.text: Piedmont football head coach Jordan Seiden called this year’s coaching staff the best in his 30 years of coaching. There’s a wealth of experience in Seiden’s second year at the school, bringing together a veteran staff that includes former longtime Bishop O’Dowd and Mt. Eden coach Paul Perenon as offensive coordinator. It also includes former Fremont of Oakland line coaches Isaac and Pauhila Tauaho. Former coordinator Mike Dixon remains an offensive assistant, while defensive coordinator Kerry Griffin and running backs coach DeMario Glenn enter their second year. Local football aficionados will know Perenon. He spent 25-years as Bishop O’Dowd’s coach from 1985-2009, then coached at Mt. Eden from 2010-2022. Seiden was an assistant and junior varsity coach at O’Dowd under Perenon. “Jordan coached our JV football team back in 2001 or 2002. I’ve just followed his career and we have kept in touch over the years. He was going to be on our staff in Mt. Eden in the fall of 2019 but some family issues precluded him being able to become our defensive coordinator. And then he got the job at Piedmont,” said Perenon. After spending 13 years as Mt. Eden’s head coach, Perenon made the decision to step down from the job due to a lack of necessary support from the Hayward school in aiding his student-athletes academically. He remains a PE teacher at Mt. Eden. “I had already set up the schedule at Mt. Eden and had full intention of continuing there, but circumstances changed,” Perenon said. “I talked with Jordan in June and he asked me how retirement was going. I told him I’m not retired, I’m just not coaching at Mt. Eden and I’d take the right situation if it came up. Jordan then invited me to their summer workouts,” said Perenon. Seiden told him that his coaching staff, including former coordinator and current offensive assistant Mike Dixon, wanted Perenon to run the offense. Perenon attended one of Piedmont’s 7-on-7 practices in June and decided to join the Highlanders soon after. Perenon enters a similar situation in Piedmont to when he joined Mt. Eden in 2010 and Bishop O’Dowd in 1985, both programs that were rebuilding. He took O’Dowd to three NCS titles in 1997, 1998 and 2004. He can take credit for helping send countless players to play in college, including Langston Walker, Burl Toler, Kirk Morrisson, and Piedmont-native Eric Bjornson, all of whom went toto play in the NFL. When starting at Mt. Coach Jim Landes and assistant coach Corey Reich are keeping watchful eyes to determine how this year’s singles and doubles lineups will resolve. Piedmont has a good cast of eight returning varsity players, but must replace five experienced layers dye to graduation, including No. 1 doubles team Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte, and No. 2 singles player Anne Jumper. “We lost a few girls who graduated and some starters, but I think overall we will be almost as strong if not as strong as last season,” said Landes. “We did very well last season; we almost won Sophomore Kate Jumper is Piedmont’s likely No. 2 singles starter. Sophomore Arianna Kortum has been impressive since joining the team last year. NCS and won the league.” Returning for her senior year and second year on the team is Tanya Kononova, the No. 1 singles player since her arrival a year ago as a refugee from Ukraine. She won last year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles tournament. She’s been competing in local tournaments, boosting her ranking as she gains more recognition from colleges. “We have Tanya back at No. 1,” confirmed Landes. “She’s better than she was last year, working hard and I’ve been helping her as much as I can, taking her to some tournaments. articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team survived a challenging game with Pierce High School in Arbuckle (Colusa County) on Friday, August 25, in their first game of the season. Despite some signs of hope, turnovers and the opposing team’s formidable running game proved to be decisive factors that contributed to a 50-0 victory for the home team. In contrast, Piedmont’s varsity played to a much more closely contested game with Pierce in a 28-21 loss. As the game kicked off, Pierce quickly took control with a running game, and scored quickly. Amidst the challenges Piedmont’s return specialists, George Bishop and Jason Shum, both made impressive returns of over 50 yards. However, Piedmont’s offense could do little to move the ball other than a 13-yard reception by Bishop and quarterback Cash Panico scrambling for 54 yards on the ground. The game unfolded under scorching conditions, with temperatures soaring to 95 degrees. This heat took a toll on Piedmont’s players, evident from fatigue shown whenever there was a break in the action. One bright spot was on Pierce’s lone passing attempt, when freshman Diego Hurwitz picked off the pass. After that Pierce never threw the ball again for the rest of the game. Defensive highlights included Cash Panico with 15 total tackles, Jason Shum eight tackles, and Nik Costello with a sack and seven tackles. In the second half, Pierce returned an interception for a touchdown and continued using its running game to exploit the Scots’ defense. articles.text: Championship water polo team returns with eyes on NCS title Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team is back for 2023 and has been completely clear on their aspirations for this year, in spite of being in the second year without a hometown pool. After winning back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference titles and two-consecutive North Coast Section semifinals appearances, the Highlanders return with their target on capturing the school’s first NCS title. “We feel like this team is capable of winning NCS, that’s our goal,” said coach Rik Krumins, entering his second year at the helm. ”We have a lot of returning talent and think we can take that next step,” Piedmont won last year’s WACC Championship over Alameda with a resounding 13-4 victory and finished the season with a 20-7 overall record. They return several key players, including Peter Krumins, Declan Linnane, George Stein, Evan Dickason, Daniel Banin, Quincy Sherman and Finn Burke – all seniors. “I think we’ll be able to be versatile; everyone in the pool can play every position. In the past, not everyone could handle the ball, pass, and shoot. Now, I think all six people can handle that. I think we’ll all be threats,” said Linnane. Krumins recalled Piedmont’s 2021 WACC title win over Berkeley, 12-8, in which Piedmont had to rely on its starters for nearly every minute of the match. With a deeper team Piedmont will be able to attack with more players. “Now we can go to our starters, then make subs and be just fine,” said Krumins. Piedmont reached the 2021 North Coast Section semifinals, losing 7-4 to No. 2 Marin Academy. Last year the Highlanders lost to the same school, 6-5. The biggest change on this year’s team will be the absence of all-league goalie Dariush Kashani, who was voted the League Player of the Year. Junior Gus von Metszch and sophomore Luke McAuliffe will be competing for the position. “Those two are competing. Gus has a lot of length and Luke has a lot of experience with club. articles.text: On Saturday, August 26 at the Laney College pool, Piedmont High School’s boys’ water polo team hosted its annual Alumni Game. It brought together players going back to the very start of the program in the early 90s. The alumni won the game 19-15 with help of the school’s all-time leading scorer Patrick Conn and all-time leading assister Henry Saunders, classmates from 2019. “It’s great to bring the community together. It seems like every year it gets bigger. We’ve had some talented teams over the years and it’s great to put our team in the pool against players like Patrick and Henry. It’s really a testament to the Piedmont water polo community,” said PHS head coach Rik Krumins, who jumped in the pool with everyone else after the game. Conn and Saunders led Piedmont in the fall of 2018 to a 22-6 overall record, but narrowly lost in the WACC Finals to Bishop O’Dowd. The team lost in the NCS Semifinals to Cardinal Newman the following year. Conn continued his career at the University of Toronto and Saunders at USC. Piedmont’s Class of 2019 marked the final team to play in the Piedmont Pool. Since then, the Highlanders have been playing on the road. The pool is being replaced by a new $19 million aquatic facility, but not until the summer of 2024. The team captured the first two League (WACC) titles in school history in 2021 and 2022. Now, PHS is looking to get over its North Coast Section hump and capture a an NCS banner. “Events like today and community building activities really brings everyone together. These events help make the program what it is today,” said senior leader George Stein. “We’re a really driven team and we want to win, but at the end of the day it’s the community that gets people here.” “It helped us to see so many great players like Henry, Patrick, and Adam [Lowe] play at Piedmont. It really inspired us to push our game to play before high school,” mentioned fellow senior Declan Linnane. PHS increased its lead to 5-3 until the Patrick Conn, Class of 2019, was a mainstay on the Alumni team. He is the school’s all-time leading scorer. In the second period, PHS surged ahead 7-5, but Saunders quickly responded for a 7-7 tie. After falling behind 8-6, Conn scored back-to-back goals to the game a 8-8. Just before halftime, the high school team scored again for a slender 9-8 edge, The teams traded goals until the Alumni took a 12-11 lead in the third quarter. At 12-12, the Alumni scored four goals to go up 16-12, the biggest margin in the game. But PHS was not done. They scored the opening three goals of the fourth period to make it a nail-biter at 16-15. Conn and Saunders re-entered the pool, and soon the scored soared to 19-15. At the end, everyone jumped in the pool for some mayhem, with more than 30 people having a great time.

articles.text: August 18 San Francisco Choral Society concert Ukraine and Mozart, an unlikely coupling indeed, paired to light up Davies Hall recently in a gratifying choral-orchestral concert under Robert Geary. Geary’s S.F. Choral Society linked with Ukrainian composer Alexander Shchetynsky, 63, from afar unveiling his Requiem (1991- 2004), a serene lyrical outpouring with string orchestra. However somber a work, the composer establishes a mellifluous flow in his work with Latin text, closer to the spirit of Brahms’ Requiem. Among his original touches was the “Lacrimosa,” with choral sound segments seemingly coming from various directions. The topper in the 25-minute piece in six traditional movements is the contrasting “Dies Irae” (Day of Wrath), a powerful outburst propelled by the SFCS’ strong soprano section. The latter work paired with Mozart’s eternal Requiem, one of the great 18th century creations even though left incomplete. Mozart wrote his final note in the “Lacrimosa,” penned right after the interval of the falling sixth in the chorus – an unusual leap, surpassed by the falling seventh of the earlier Kyrie, perhaps symbolizing his own premature departure. Though an amateur ensemble like most of our choruses, this group of some 130 voices carried off the performance, even if slighting the consonants the way that even our leading professional chorus consistently does. (Yes, folks, Latin, like most European languages needs audible consonants even more than English.) The high point of the performance was in the closely linked vocal quartet of contrasting voice types, skillfully coached by Geary. Who could resist their “Benedictus,” an evocative passage partly attributable to the collaborative composer (and Mozart pupil) Franz Suessmayr? The concert, filling only about a half of Davies Hall, was in part a fund-raising event for the Ukraine’s Kharkiv National University of the Arts, damaged by rockets during the recent wartime bombings. It is located where Shchetynsky was born and currently teaches. The SF Choral Society had been in touch with the composer via Zoom in preparing this rare concert. Choral Society The Mozart soloists were Emily Sinclair, Shauna Fallihee, Michael Jankosky and Eugene Brancoveanu, paired with the SFCS Summer Festival Chorus. The two-person play by Liz Duffy Adams stars Dean Linnard as poet and English spy Kit Marlowe and Brady Morales-Woolery as Will Shakespeare, an upstart looking to make his name in the world of art. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s Hippest Trip - The Soul Train Musical is currently playing at the Toni Rembe Theater, 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Soul Train is based on the iconic TV show that originally aired on Chicago airwaves in the 1970’s. For over 30 years, it brought Black music, dance, and style into living rooms in America and was a celebration of black youth culture. The show’s self-proclaimed reputation was “the hippest trip in America,” hence the musical’s title. The creative team behind ACT’s reimagined Soul Train includes Tony Award–nominated playwright Dominique Morisseau known for The Detroit Project, Tony Award–nominated choreographer Camille A. Brown, and the Apollo Theater’s executive director Kamilah Forbes. Playwright Morisseau said she is looking forward to partnering with an all-female creative team to celebrate “the history and unsung heroes of our nation’s longest running televised music and dance series.” “I am so excited to help bring the narrative of one of our culture’s most influential and legend-making endeavors to the stage. Having grown up on this series and being immersed in the culture around it, I never knew what it took to make it the iconic staple that it is,” she said. The cast includes Angela Birchett as Delores, Quentin Earl Darrington as Don Cornelius, Amber Iman as Pam Brown, and Kayla Davion as Jody Watley. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/soul-train/.

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) opens a new, permanent collection exhibition entitled Sea Change on Saturday, September 2, with photographer and Piedmonter Reagan Louie among the featured artists. Sea Change features works by Takashi Arai, Jonathan Calm, Tina Barney, Guanyu Xu, and Zoe Strauss, as well as solo presentations of work by Ilse Bing and Louie. Speaking on the show, Louie said “The exhibition’s title is an expression that denotes a dramatic change, a paradigm shift… I’m delighted to be in this timely show about the global transitional moment we are in. The monographic presentation of my work explores China during [the 1980s], arguably the most transformative period in its modern history.” While his father was born in a village in Guangdong, China, Louie is a fifth-generation Californian on his mother’s side and often cites this contrast and the challenges of assimilating between two developing, often competing societies as a major influence on his work. “The photographs reveal China’s emergence from the slumber of the Cultural Revolution to become a global superpower,” Louie added. Among the works to be featured in his solo presentation is “Birdman” from his Beijing, 1987 series, pictured above. Overall, the new collection at SFMOMA explores how modern photography bears witness to political and environmental shifts over time. The exhibition is presented as a suite of thematic and monographic galleries, mainly focused on waterways and oceans. The works of photography are by over 50 under-recognized artists from around the world. The exhibition will be on view through February 19, 2024. To learn more, visit sfmoma. org/exhibition/sea-change-photographs-from-the-collection. “Birdman,” from Piedmonter and photographer Reagan Louie’s Beijing 1987 series of photos. Sea Change features works by Takashi Arai, Jonathan Calm, Tina Barney, Guanyu Xu, and Zoe Strauss, as well as solo presentations of work by Ilse Bing and Louie. Speaking on the show, Louie said “The exhibition’s title is an expression that denotes a dramatic change, a paradigm shift… I’m delighted to be in this timely show about the global transitional moment we are in. The monographic presentation of my work explores China during [the 1980s], arguably the most transformative period in its modern history.” While his father was born in a village in Guangdong, China, Louie is a fifth-generation Californian on his mother’s side and often cites this contrast and the challenges of assimilating between two developing, often competing societies as a major influence on his work. “The photographs reveal China’s emergence from the slumber of the Cultural Revolution to become a global superpower,” Louie added. Among the works to be featured in his solo presentation is “Birdman” from his Beijing, 1987 series, pictured above. Overall, the new collection at SFMOMA explores how modern photography bears witness to political and environmental shifts over time. The exhibition is presented as a suite of thematic and monographic galleries, mainly focused on waterways and oceans. The works of photography are by over 50 under-recognized artists from around the world. The exhibition will be on view through February 19, 2024. To learn more, visit sfmoma. org/exhibition/sea-change-photographs-from-the-collection. “Birdman,” from Piedmonter and photographer Reagan Louie’s Beijing 1987 series of photos. Louie is among 50 artists from around the world to be featured in Sea Change, a new, permanent collection exhibition at SFMOMA on view now through February 2024. articles.text: Music preview by Paul Hertelendy One of the newest and most versatile early-music singing groups locally is Tactus SF, now seven years old, affiliated with the San Francisco Early Music Society. Mention “early music” and you expect to hear polyphonic chorales from Europe. Not so, this time. This 20-member a cappella group put together an entire program of early New-World music, “Cantus Mexicanus,” digging out sacred renaissance choral music of “New Spain,” as it was then called, It is music we almost never get to hear, part of it sung in indigenous languages. One of the beauties of Bay Area residence is the chance to hear concerts with a broader repertoire, whether instrumental or vocal. The Tactus discovery trip transpired August 27 at St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Berkeley, with the added asset of a period wind instruments trio, with some singers doubling as instrumentalists. Music Director Elizabeth Kimble has assembled a varied group, notable both for its versatility and its resounding lyric sopranos, to perform half-forgotten 16th- and 17th-century selections. The most accomplished of all these composers were two that started in Spain and emigrated to take on church posts in Mexico. Gutierréz de Padilla was a master polyphonist running the cathedral in Puebla. (Here, with two of his brief Latin excerpts, “Vidi turbam” and “Stabat mater.”) Even more remarkable was Hernando Franco, choirmaster in Mexico City less than a century after Columbus’ first New-World discovery journey. The implication is that he produced good works and performers for worship in record time. Besides the Latin, the polyglot ensemble Tactus also performed in local languages like Nahuatl and Peruvian Quechua, both ballasted by intimidating five-syllable words. Of special note was one of the Old-Testament Lamentations of Jeremiah portraying the suffering of the people, composed by the indigenous Juan de Lienas. Instrumental works by Bravo and Gaspar Fernandes featured Renaissance cornetto, sackbut and dulcian. Given the direction of repertory here, then certainly a future program of music from our California missions would be appropriate, particularly delving into the archives of Mission San Jose in Fremont, which developed some of the finest music programs of all the West Coast missions in the early 19th century under Fr. Narcisco Durán. Tactus SF, a Bay Area unaccompanied mixed chorus under Elizabeth Kimble, performing Aug. 26 and 27 on each side of the Bay, the latter at St. Mark’s Episcopal, 2300 Bancroft, Berkeley. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, August 30, 2023 The Musical Gourmet Culinary delight By Joseph Gold The show is about to begin. Dim the lights. Cue the dramatic music. Cue the mellifluous voiced announcer. Cue the goosebumps up and down your spine. You are about to enjoy the greatest dinner you have ever experienced. That was the scene last Thursday. The stars were celebrity chef Alessandro Stratta and sommelier Erik Segelbaum. The stage was set on a large wooden deck under a canopy of giant redwoods. A Mozart string quartet began the evening as appetizers were passed around. What happened next almost defies description. But let me try. The first course was marinated Hiramasa with Osetra caviar. This was served as a salad along side chilled cucumbers, and Yuzu Sabayon. A Forjas del Salnes, Rias Baixas, (Spain 2020) was the selected wine. The second course was roasted sea scallops atop cauliflower purée with shiitake mushrooms in an aged sherry brown butter sauce. What a delightful change it is to have a cauliflower purée instead of prosaic mashed potatoes. Surprisingly, caulif lower purée is very easy to prepare. Cortina Alta Chardonnay (Mendoza, Argentina, 2019) was the selected wine. Our third course was a spectacular warm duck salad served in three variations. This dish The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet featured a large portion of duck foie gras accompanied by shredded duck breast atop a wedge of toast with a side of roasted apples and grapes. Strangely enough, a Mount Carmel Pinot noir (Rita Hills, 2019) was the choice of wine here. But can you believe it – those were the preliminaries. Roasted Sea Bass with celery root and black truffle was the first main course. The selected wine was a unique Vin d’Ambre Sauvignon Blanc (Anderson, Valley, 2019. Then came the second main course, which was an herbcrusted rack of lamb with honey-stewed peppers, garlic butter, and a basil–citrus chutney. Once again, the side course of honey stewed peppers was a delightful surprise. And once again, the preparation for this colorful side dish is surprisingly easy. As dinner progressed, sommelier Erik Segelbaum explained his choices of wines and included some side comments about the food we were enjoying. The first dessert was Epoisses cheese with spice-roasted peach crostini. Sandeman, a 10-year old Tawney port from the Douro Valley in Portugal was the ideal dessert wine. A bowl of chocolate Mezcal truffle candies sent us into the beyond. Plating for the dinner was very simple with white dishes and simple wine glasses. While this dinner was spectacular beyond belief, you can have great success at home if you serve just one of the salads and one of the warm dishes as a main course. Your success is guaranteed! Chef Alessandro Stratta is a James Beard award winner. articles.text: The Broadcast Legends “OldTime Radio Players” will bring Golden Memories of Radio to Piedmont on Sunday afternoon, September 17, at 4:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. “The Old Time Radio Players” and technical crew will re-create examples of radio newscasts, kids’ shows, daytime Soap Operas, bloopers, commercials, jingles, plus the main event, a complete episode of “The Lone Ranger.” It’s a nostalgic presentation that will take audience members back to a time when “radio was king” and the “theatre of the mind” captured our imaginations. Broadcast Legends was founded over 30 years ago and boasts over 200 members – radio and television professionals who have worked in the broadcast industry for at least 20 years. “The Old Time Radio Players” serves as the Legends’ community outreach ar m, bringing the fun and excitement of live radio to appreciative audiences throughout the Bay Area. The cast includes Michael Bennett, Peter Cleaveland, Carolyn Compton, Matt Elmore, Bruce Jenett, Jason Nunan, Hoyt Smith, and Zachary Wilson. The Technical Director is Bob Brown.

articles.text: French-American duo to perform a Friday night concert A guitar-percussion duo concert by Arthur Dente and Steve Robertson will take place at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, September 16 at 7 p.m. Advance tickets at $20 are available at https://bpt. me/6124713, or $25 at the door - cash or checks only. Arthur Dente is a French guitarist, composer and performer, trained in both classical and improvised music. Of Portuguese origin, his compositions develop an interaction between the Iberian Peninsula, Europe and, by extension, world cultures. A gold medalist in classical guitar at the Montauban Conservatory, he studied composition and music history at the Toulouse Conservatory, then at the École Normale de Musique de Paris.. He holds a degree in musicology from the University of Aix-en-Provence, where he was a lecturer for several years. He obtained the CAPES, a State diploma that enabled him to teach music education and put his compositions into practice with students in music specialization. • Nominated for the CEMF (French music publishers’ union) competition, for writing a contemporary work, on May 28, 2023. Guitarist & composer Arthur Dente • • • Participation as solo guitarist in the show « LA PÉPINIÈRE DES COMPOSITEURS », in Aix-en-Provence on June 5 and 6, 2023.Solo concert in Paris on June 17, 2023. Duo concert: Guitar & Cello, given in Balogna, South Corsica, on July 11, 2023. Participation in the « LES SUPERPHONIQUES » 2023 • Percussionist Steve Robertson contemporary music competition, writing a piece for choir, guitar and flute. Participation in the CEMF 2024 competition in the Repertoire category for the writing of a piece for orchestra accompanied by its musicological analysis. Percussionist Steve Robertson has been active performing, recording, producing and teaching in the Bay Area for more than 25 years. A graduate of San Jose State University with a BA in Music Performance and Education. He has performed and recorded in a variety of musical styles with artists including Bobby Hutcherson, Airto and Flora Purim, Laurindo Almeida, Claudia Villela, Othello Molineaux, Giovanni Hidalgo, Omar Sosa, John Calloway, Arthur Dente and many others. His musical focus is primarily in Jazz and World Music styles including Brazilian, Afro-Cuban and North Indian Classical music (on tabla). He studied orchestral percussion with Anthony Cirone at SJSU and is a tabla student of Ustad Zakir Hussain. He has also performed on percussion with the Monterey and Santa Cruz County Symphonies.

articles.text: Summer Hours is an award winning film from France. Summer Hours, written and directed by Oliver Assayas, is a film with an almost imperceptible narrative arc, a film absent moments of great tension, high drama, or irreparable confrontation. Instead, it is a film that mirrors life in all its subtlety and nuanced moments. articles.text: Luca, the 24th animated feature from Pixar, opened absent a wide theater release and is therefore now streaming. It is a comingof-age story set in the Italian seaside village of Portorosso, on the sun-washed Riviera. It’s a place of dreamy blues, soft oranges, and inviting yellows. The time is in the 1950s and 1960s. At the center of the tale is Luca Paguro (Jacob Tremblay), a restless tween-teen who is a sea monster. He lives with his extended sea monster family in an underwater world. There’s Daniela, his mom (Maya Rudolph); Lorenzo Paguro, his dad (Jim Gaffigan); Grandma Paguro (Sandy Martin); and Uncle Ugo (Sacha Baron Cohn). Plus Luca’s new best friend, also a sea monster, Alberto Scorfario (Jack Dylan Grazer). The interesting twist is that when Luca and Alberto venture on shore they turn into regular boys who look like everyone else. And it’s on land where they discover that though they were warned by their families that the town of Portorosso could be dangerous, the boys find it filled with interesting, eye-widening possibilities. And so, the two set off on an irresistible adventure in where they meet a cast of interesting characters, to include a feisty girl, Giulia Marcovaldo (Emma Berman), and her good-hearted fisherman/cook father, Massimo Marcovaldo (Marco Barricelli). They enter an annual Vespa race, take countless Vespa rides around town, confront the town bully, Saverio Raimondo (Ercole Visconti) – he was the previous winner of the Vespa race medal – and, along the way, learn the meaning of true friendship. The animation is delightful, the palette of detail and colors extraordinary. And the filmmakers acknowledge the influence of the iconic Japanese Studio Ghibli and the creative genius of animator and storyteller Hayao Miyazaki. Luca is a wonderful, imaginative story that should engage a wide audience of kids who will find Luca, both the sea monster and the boy, compelling. Luca. Pixar/Disney animation. Directed by Enrico Casarosa. Voices by Jacob Tremblay, Jack Dylan Grazer, Emma Berman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Disney+/Apple tv. A scene from Pixar’s Luca

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays walkers knew the temperature would be high as they assembled on August 23. A hearty group of 45 walkers and one K-9 best friend were on hand to see something special. Retired architect Chuck Oraftik had offered the group an opportunity to see the large and highly detailed model railroad he has built in the basement of his Oakland Avenue home. This visit would be a shorter walk and offer a fun activity on a hot day. The walkers headed off going down Magnolia Avenue past the construction for the new Piedmont Aquatics Center. Peak holes in the construction fence allowed walkers to make inspections. The group continued down Magnolia past El Cerrito Avenue where EBMUD has been repairing a critical water pipeline leak. The group turned down Oakland Avenue and quickly came to Chuck’s house, which had a temporary railroad crossing sign in front. Chuck came out to greet them and a group photo was taken. They went down the driveway to a garage area where Chuck had chairs and beverages waiting for them. In response to a question, Chuck recounted the origins of both his train fascination and his architectural career. When he was a young boy most of his earliest toys were building/construction related, starting with tinker toys. , over the years they became more complex and sophisticated - slowly developing the technological, research, construction, artistic and planning skills required for an architectural career and for a historically accurate scale model railroad. His basement is a “time machine” from the 1950s in upper New York state. There is heavy freight and passenger train traffic on his HO scale version of the Boston & Albany Division of the New York Central railroad. The trains pass through the Berkshire Hills in route to Pittsfield, Mass. Chatham, N.Y. and, eventually, Albany N.Y. Along the way are small villages, industries, downtowns, swiftly moving rivers and hillsides forested with some 4,000 detailed trees. All locomotives have been equipped with sophisticated integrated circuits that control locomotive sounds, momentum, and speed. The steam locomotives have synchronized smoke effects. In addition, all locomotives, rolling stock, buildings, automobiles, and scenery are “weathered” to create a realistic, muted appearance and to eliminate a resemblance of toy trains. To ensure his work not be destroyed if it ever needs to be moved, his model railroad is built in large modules that can be separated with minimal damage. Chuck has been working on his model railroad for some 20 years. This phase one measures about 400 square feet. He has recently begun planning a second phase which will almost double its size. The large number of walkers and the confined aisle space allowed only a dozen at a time to view his trains. It took about 40 minutes for everyone to see his elaborate layout. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: World famous anthropologist and conservationist Jane Goodall will appear in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist and activist Goodall will discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960. Her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of the evening. Visit https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/ to purchase tickets. pages.text: Wednesday, August 30, 2023 23 Golden Gate Theatre welcomes Jane Goodall on Sept. 15 By Allyson Aleksey World famous anthropologist and conservationist Jane Goodall will appear in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist and activist Goodall will discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960. Her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of the evening. Visit https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/ to purchase tickets. World famous anthropologist and conservationist Jane Goodall will appear in San Francisco on September 15. READ IT IN THE POST How will you exit your business? If you own a business, you’ve always got a lot on your mind. But no matter how busy you are today, you need to think about tomorrow. Specifically, you’ll want to create an exit strategy for the day you want to move on from your business to a new phase in your life. To develop this strategy, you’ll need to address these key questions: • How much do you need (or want) for your business? Ideally, you’ll want the sale of your business to meet your retirement and estate-planning goals. So, you’ll need to think carefully about these goals and what costs they may entail. And these issues aren’t just financial ­ – for example, when you think about how you may want to spend your time in retirement, you might realize that you don’t really want to exit your business completely. So, you might decide to sell just part of it, or sell it entirely, but stay on to help manage it or possibly do some consulting for the new owners. • How much is your business worth? You may want to calculate your business’ value three to five years before your planned exit. You could do this on your own, but it’s typically advantageous to use professional valuation services. If you’re gifting or selling your business to family members, selling it to an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) or settling an estate, you’ll need to get a more formal qualified appraisal to meet IRS standards. • How can you close the gap between what you need and what your business is worth? The amount you need from the sale of your business to support your retirement goals may be more than what your business is actually worth. To help close this gap, you could try to boost your business’s profits through the usual means, such as introducing new products, raising prices or cutting costs. But you might also try to lower the amount you need from the sale by working longer, reducing your personal spending and saving more outside the business. • Who will take over your business? When planning for a successor for your business, you have several choices, including selling to a family member or an outside buyer. Going public or liquidating the business are also options. These are distinct paths, but depending on your circumstances, one might be more appropriate for you than another. To cite just one factor, if you don’t have an obvious choice for a family member to take over the business, you might have to consider other buyers. In any case, you’ll need to explore all the economic and personal factors involved in the choice of successor. • Who can help you with your exit strategy? Exiting a business can be complex. To ensure you’re making the right moves for your overall financial and family situations, you may want to build an exit strategy team, possibly consisting of your financial, legal and tax advisors. You may also need to enlist the services of a commercial banker and a business evaluation expert. Each of these professionals can bring a different area of expertise to your exit decisions, and together they can help address all the issues related to your exit strategy. Exiting your business will take a lot of planning and decisions — but if it’s done right, it can be worth the effort. .This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: During a brief respite from the intense summer heat, 14 members of the Piedmont Seniors took an excursion to the picturesque town of Saratoga to visit the breathtaking Villa Montalvo estate. Built in 1912 by Senator James Phelan, who was also a three-term mayor of San Francisco, this 177- acre gem is an Italian Mediterranean Revival mansion. It was Phelan’s favorite home and became a center of artistic, political, and social Pictured are (clockwise from left): Yorkman Lowe, Carol Warren, Madeline Moore, Mona Jamieson, Penny Robb, Diane Frost, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska life in Northern California. Some of Phelan’s well-known guest celebrities included Jack London, Ethel Barrymore, Mary Pickford, and Douglass Fairbanks. Montalvo sits near the Santa Cruz mountains surrounded by exquisite gardens and an arboretum. Since 1939 Montalvo opened as a public arts center and is part of the County Park System, so it is available for visitors to explore. Montalvo is home to the oldest artists residency program of its kind west of the Mississippi. The organization hosts more than 60 artists from over 17 countries active in the visual arts, dance, literature, music, and the culinary arts. Montalvo also has a small gallery in the Villa. It is now a park with hiking trails, in addition to being a very popular venue for weddings and other events, complete with an outdoor 1600- seat amphitheater for concerts and other cultural events. As the Villa is quite expensive to maintain, the Montalvo Service Group offers catered “summer luncheons” as a major charity benefit to continue the preservation of this magnificent property. The Montalvo Organization also hosts a Mother’s Day Brunch, Yuletide, Madhatters Tea for children, and Gourmet Dinners at the Villa. On this occasion, the Piedmont Seniors were treated to a gourmet lunch consisting of a crispy polenta appetizer with ricotta and truffle honey, the entrée of Tuscan roasted chicken stuffed with spinach, herbs, and cheese., and a lemon raspberry trifle consisting of layers of fresh lemon curd, baked shortbread cookies and raspberry whipped cream! While the Seniors were enjoying their luncheon under the shade of a large front veranda, Montalvo volunteers hosted an informal fashion show by Chicos’ women’s apparel. This outstanding property is a “must-see” for anyone interested in natural beauty and historic architecture. Needless to say, the Piedmont Seniors were most impressed by this “hidden gem” tucked away in the hills of Saratoga. articles.text: On Saturday, August 12, a gorgeous summer day, 22 excited seniors took a three-hour cruise aboard the historic USS Potomac on San Francisco Bay. The tour began with a 20-minute video giving a brief history of the USS Potomac. The tour included a box lunch and allowed time to leisurely explore the famous presidential yacht. Shorter two-hour tours without lunch are also available to the public. The USS Potomac, which is docked conveniently in Jack London Square at the Oakland Estuary, encourages visitors to come aboard and learn the history of this famous vessel. On the day the Seniors arrived there was a special narration about World War II. The Seniors were fortunate enough to have a docent explain some of the areas of the presidential yacht, such as the private quarters of FDR, the engine room, and officers’ quarters. The vessel was President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s yacht on which he was able to relax and entertain visitors, including kings and queens, until his death in 1945. This yacht is a living memorial to President Roosevelt and a testament to the challenges he overcame as a polio victim and during one of the most stressful times in American history. As Secretary of Navy prior to becoming President, he had a special affinity for the sea, unlike his wife, Eleanor, who rarely accompanied her husband on his sailings. The USS Potomac has an unusual history. It was initially commissioned as a Coast Guard Cutter in 1934 and was renamed in 1936 as the USS Potomac. Elvis Presley owned the ship briefly. He transferred ownership to Danny Thomas for St. Jude’s Foundation. Later it fell into disrepair when the next group of owners were using it to smuggle drugs. Soon it was seized by the federal government, but sank in the cove at Treasure Island. Fortunately, the vessel was rescued and purchased for $15,000 by the Port of Oakland at auction, with no other bidders. After the purchase, the process of restoration began by the Potomac Association, a 501c3 non-profit organization, to turn the yacht into a floating museum. An interesting sidenote of the yacht is its simplicity. It is nothing fancy or luxurious that one might expect a President to own. You can visit FDR’s bedroom, bathroom and the quarters for the crew and executive officers as well as the dining room. The recently hired Executive Director of the USS Potomac is Ford Roosevelt, son of Elliott Roosevelt and grandson to FDR. Ford brings a special knowledge of the family history and a dedication to see that this presidential yacht retains its integrity. Today the USS Potomac is used for Bay cruises, dockside tours on specific Saturdays and Sundays, private charters, and student cruises. For more information, see usspotomac.org or call (510) 627-1215. After disembarking the USS Potomac the Piedmont Seniors posed for a group photo. Not pictured: Patti Singer.

articles.text: Consideration of Amendments to Piedmont City Code and to Piedmont Design Guidelines to Implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards and Accessory Dwelling Unit Incentives Notice is hereby given that the City of Piedmont City Council will conduct a public hearing at a regular meeting at 6:00 pm on Tuesday, September 5, 2023 in Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA, to consider the following actions: (1) consideration of an ordinance amending the Piedmont City Code to add a Pre-approved Plans incentive for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS), add ministerial review procedures, and make other conforming changes; and (2) consideration of amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code include amendments to Division 17.38, Accessory Dwelling Units, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use, including new incentives for rent-restricted ADUs for applicants using new City-approved plans for ADUs. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code also include the establishment of a new Division 17.67, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use to establish procedures and standards for ministerial review of multifamily and mixed-use building types, and other conforming changes. Proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines include: (1) new objective standards for architectural elements to be used by City staff to review development applications for multifamily and mixed-use building types; (2) pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units (ADUs); (3) renaming the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines as to “Piedmont Design Standards and Guidelines”; and (4) other conforming changes. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The amendments to address pre-approved architectural plans for ADUs are statutorily exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21080.17 and CEQA Guidelines section 15282(h) which exempts adoption of ordinances to implement Government Code section 65852.2 regarding accessory dwelling units. These amendments are also exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303.The amendments related to Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) are exempt because it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the adoption of MODS may have a significant effect on the environment. (Public Resources Code section 21065; CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Sections 15061(b)(3), 15378.) Further, these amendments are exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303. On August 14, 2023, the Planning Commission recommended City Council adoption of the amendments to the City Code and to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are available for public review on the City’s webpage at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. They are also available at City Hall located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. INTERESTED PERSONS MAY be heard at the public hearing, and written comments may be submitted prior to the public hearing(s). Written comments will be made a part of the public record. If you challenge this matter in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone else raised at the public hearing, described in this noticed, or in written correspondence, delivered to the City of Piedmont at or prior to the public hearing. You may choose to write your opinion and address the response to the Piedmont City Council via email at citycouncil@ piedmont.ca.gov or via U.S. Mail at Piedmont City Council, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. All City Council meetings are televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and will be available through streaming video on the City’s website https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/meeting_videos The City of Piedmont will publish the meeting agenda not less than 72 hours prior to the meeting. The agenda will be posted at City Hall and Police Department bulletin boards. The agenda will be available online at: https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city_council/meeting_information___agendas QUESTIONS AND INQUIRIES regarding this matter, or to review information for the project described above, can be directed to: Pierce Macdonald Senior Planner pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov • (510) 420-3050 Originally Posted on August 18, 2023 Piedmont Post newspaper Routes currently available for weekly & monthly routes. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, August 30, 2023 PUBLIC HEARING NOTICE Consideration of Amendments to Piedmont City Code and to Piedmont Design Guidelines to Implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards and Accessory Dwelling Unit Incentives Notice is hereby given that the City of Piedmont City Council will conduct a public hearing at a regular meeting at 6:00 pm on Tuesday, September 5, 2023 in Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA, to consider the following actions: (1) consideration of an ordinance amending the Piedmont City Code to add a Pre-approved Plans incentive for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS), add ministerial review procedures, and make other conforming changes; and (2) consideration of amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code include amendments to Division 17.38, Accessory Dwelling Units, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use, including new incentives for rent-restricted ADUs for applicants using new City-approved plans for ADUs. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code also include the establishment of a new Division 17.67, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use to establish procedures and standards for ministerial review of multifamily and mixed-use building types, and other conforming changes. Proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines include: (1) new objective standards for architectural elements to be used by City staff to review development applications for multifamily and mixed-use building types; (2) pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units (ADUs); (3) renaming the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines as to “Piedmont Design Standards and Guidelines”; and (4) other conforming changes. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The amendments to address pre-approved architectural plans for ADUs are statutorily exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21080.17 and CEQA Guidelines section 15282(h) which exempts adoption of ordinances to implement Government Code section 65852.2 regarding accessory dwelling units. These amendments are also exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303.The amendments related to Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) are exempt because it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the adoption of MODS may have a significant effect on the environment. (Public Resources Code section 21065; CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Sections 15061(b)(3), 15378.) Further, these amendments are exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303. On August 14, 2023, the Planning Commission recommended City Council adoption of the amendments to the City Code and to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. We too get lonely, catastrophe seems to be ever present, we don’t have the luxury of being stupid, massive change buffets us, we need adequate rest, media seems to dominate us and it all adds up. In her essay, “Why Does Everyone Feel So Insecure All the Time?”, Astra Taylor put it this way. “We are all, to varying degrees, overwhelmed and apprehensive, fearful of what the future might have in store. We are on guard, anxious, incomplete and exposed to risk. To cope, we scramble and strive, shoring ourselves up against potential threats. We work hard, shop hard, hustle, get credentialed, scrimp and save, invest, diet, self-medicate, meditate, exercise, exfoliate. And yet, security, for the most part, eludes us.” Jesus, seemed to know that like us, the people of his world were burdened by rampant insecurity. His answers were to “do unto others as you would they do unto you,” to love our neighbors as ourselves, to seek forgiveness as well as to be forgiving and to set aside time for prayer. He urged all who were “weary and heavy laden” to come to him. He promised that his burden would be light.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, August 30, 2023 Religion Corner Continued from page 2 part, describe our lives as well? We too get lonely, catastrophe seems to be ever present, we don’t have the luxury of being stupid, massive change buffets us, we need adequate rest, media seems to dominate us and it all adds up. In her essay, “Why Does Everyone Feel So Insecure All the Time?”, Astra Taylor put it this way. “We are all, to varying degrees, overwhelmed and apprehensive, fearful of what the future might have in store. We are on guard, anxious, incomplete and exposed to risk. To cope, we scramble and strive, shoring ourselves up against potential threats. We work hard, shop hard, hustle, get credentialed, scrimp and save, invest, diet, self-medicate, meditate, exercise, exfoliate. And yet, security, for the most part, eludes us.” Jesus, seemed to know that like us, the people of his world were burdened by rampant insecurity. His answers were to “do unto others as you would they do unto you,” to love our neighbors as ourselves, to seek forgiveness as well as to be forgiving and to set aside time for prayer. He urged all who were “weary and heavy laden” to come to him. He promised that his burden would be light. I don’t profess to understand all that his invitation means. At the very least I think it means that Jesus sees our insecurity both as a threat to our well-being and as an opportunity – an opportunity to be vulnerable, to be honest about our situation and to recognize that the better way we seek was lived by a Palestinian Jew residing in the shadow of the Roman Empire in a time long ago. A time when people like him did not have the luxury of being stupid.
